title: The "Blueprint" for Authenticity: How Official AI Protects Image and Likeness in the Digital Age (Dave Siegfried, CEO)
author: Dave Siegfried

dom.t: Pragmatic adoption: Experimentation outruns transformation evidence

st.t: Legal software: Workflow layers defend specialist value
st.an: The source concerns an authenticity and likeness product rather than software for performing legal work. Its emphasis on adapting to evolving law and validating an idea through stakeholder conversations is only tangentially relevant to governance and practitioner feedback; it does not address specialist legal workflow layers, lawyer–engineer collaboration, human verification, or copilot deployment.
qs: Those laws continue to evolve at the state, the federal, the global level, but that's why we really thought, okay, we can build technology that allows for us to work within the confines of those laws and evolve as those laws do.
But in that first meeting, I walked out and just started dialing musicians and athletes, and celebrities that I have access to, and just start asking them what they thought.

st.t: Pragmatic adoption: Experimentation outruns transformation evidence
st.an: Siegfried exemplifies pragmatic, feedback-led AI development: client conversations inform Official AI’s roadmap and attorneys are invited to shape the product. His claims concern product-building and expansion ambitions, without comparative performance measures or demonstrated transformational outcomes.
qs: There's eight of us total on the team right now, and the majority of that team are engineers, with myself and a few others meeting with clients and translating that into product feedback to drive our roadmap.
Pull up a chair, take a seat at the table, help us build the right product.

kp.k: Authenticity rests on consent, not absence of AI
kp.d: Siegfried frames Official AI's purpose as enabling people and brands to create synthetic images and video with consent, credit and compensation for name, image, likeness and voice. His thesis defines authenticity through authorization of the message rather than whether media were generated artificially; this is a vendor's stated approach, not an independently tested finding.
qs: And by authentic content, I mean using AI to create images and video while ensuring consent, credit, and compensation for the use of one's name, image, likeness, and voice.
Our thesis is that synthetic media can be authentic media, if you can verify that there was consent given for the message.

kp.k: Publicity rights offer an alternative to training-data disputes
kp.d: Siegfried explicitly excludes underlying training-data copyright questions from the company's focus. Anticipating that those disputes will eventually be resolved through markets and courts, he describes a nearer-term strategy of building technology around US publicity rights and image rights elsewhere, adapting as laws evolve. His broad characterization of likeness protections is his assertion, not a jurisdiction-specific legal finding.
qs: Yes, although we aren't focused on the underlying training data.

We took the position that this is going to be solved at some point in the market, through the courts, but there's a need immediately to provide a proactive solution that allows us to leverage our name, image likeness, and voice, and that's what we built with Official AI.
We really leaned into its right of publicity in the states, image rights elsewhere.

Those laws continue to evolve at the state, the federal, the global level, but that's why we really thought, okay, we can build technology that allows for us to work within the confines of those laws and evolve as those laws do.

kp.k: Blueprints enable controlled synthetic production and collaboration
kp.d: Siegfried says the platform can map an individual's likeness from as few as 10 phone images, generate new images and video, and incorporate voice models. Customers can retain their blueprint without using it, create content internally, or collaborate with trusted brands. He presents this as a way to supplement photography or produce timely campaigns despite talent availability and scheduling constraints; no performance evaluation is supplied.
qs: Looking at as few as 10 images from your phone, we can create a detailed mapping of who Chad is.
We can use that to create new versions of images and use those images to create video, layer in voice models, and create content that you've approved.
We have customers who keep that Blueprint locked up.
We allow them to create that content within our own system, and they can use a variety of different text to image or video models to do that.

They can collaborate with the brand to create content that's complimentary to existing photography or is brand new, allowing them to tell new stories, to create culturally relevant, timely content, to be in the conversation when the conversation is being held, even if new content can't be created.

kp.k: Layered provenance links content to authorization
kp.d: Siegfried describes a layered provenance approach beginning with C2PA manifests and supplemented by cryptographic signatures, watermarking, fingerprinting and perceptual hashes. These mechanisms are presented as ways to disclose origins and changes, signal alteration and establish authenticity. The transcript describes product capabilities and possible approaches rather than measured detection accuracy or resistance to circumvention.
qs: So every piece of content that comes through our platform, we take a layered approach to provenance. So it starts with C2PA.
So it's an open source standard that allows anyone to view a manifest of where content originated, changes to that content, where it's supposed to live.
And then layering in different cryptographic signatures, watermarking, fingerprinting, perceptual hash.
There's a variety of different approaches that we can take to signal whether content's been altered or verify that the content's authentic.

kp.k: Licensing metadata supports ongoing rights administration
kp.d: Siegfried says users can upload or point to content on Official AI's website to retrieve associated C2PA data and basic licensing information. He describes license status and duration as relevant to whether content should remain available and whether an artist should receive further compensation for continued use. This is a claimed rights-administration mechanism, not evidence that payment or removal occurs automatically.
qs: You can come to the Official AI website and upload or point to a piece of content.
We're going to provide the C2PA data associated with that image.

And then we're also sharing the basic licensing details. Is this licensed? Should this still be up? You know, was it only available for a year? And the artist needs to be made whole for its continued use.

kp.d: Siegfried positions Official AI on the proactive side of a toolkit that also needs takedown services. Drawing an analogy with music distribution, he calls it an iTunes-like response to demand for new uses, intended to make authorized participation practicable for those who want to comply. The mechanism is prevention through consent-based workflows, not a claim to eliminate unauthorized activity.
qs: I think that there needs to be a proactive and reactive set of tools, and we are definitely on the proactive side.
So let's prevent misuse for everyone that wants to do the right thing, which I believe is the majority.
So I think of us as the iTunes to generative AI shift, the proper correct way to ensure consent, credit and compensation for everyone involved.
the takedown services that live on the other side of the equation that you need in your toolkit as well, handle removal of the content that's not genuine.

kp.k: Current takedown systems struggle with synthetic likeness misuse
kp.d: Siegfried argues that users currently face difficult reporting processes and limited access to the appropriate platform staff. He characterizes existing mechanisms as designed for earlier problems and liability mitigation rather than effective removal of generative-AI likeness misuse. Separately, he predicts that social and video platforms will soon check authenticity at upload before distribution; he does not report that this future workflow is already generally operating.
qs: Yeah. So that's usually done by the user. And the truth is, today, it's a difficult process to navigate.

Generative AI is such a huge shift that the tools in place on a lot of the platforms, which were really meant to mitigate liability, aren't effective tools to remove content that is blatantly misusing one's likeness.
And what's even more difficult in that scenario is getting the attention of the right person or department at a major platform that's uploading thousands and thousands of hours of content per minute.
And I believe that will occur at the platform level soon, where if you're uploading content to TikTok or Insta or YouTube, they're looking for that verification.

kp.k: Open authentication must preserve confidential licensing terms
kp.d: Responding to the host's blockchain proposal, Siegfried distinguishes accessibility from confidentiality: closed systems restrict who can authenticate content, while open blockchains may reveal information that should remain private. He advocates a layered open-source approach without blockchain today and speculates about a future hybrid providing an immutable, accessible record while protecting underlying license details.
qs: So if you're using a proprietary closed blockchain that only one platform has access to, then only that platform is able to verify that the content is authentic.
If it's open, you're potentially giving away information that shouldn't be part of that authentication process.
And that licensing information, it's important to know it was licensed. This is authentic, but the underlying details of that license shouldn't be available to the general public.
So that's where today we really believe that there's a layered open source approach that doesn't require blockchain.
But in the future, I think there's a hybrid approach that provides all of us with that immutable open source record that's needed for verification.

kp.k: Attorneys participate in designing authorized AI uses
kp.d: Siegfried describes working with talent and their attorneys to determine appropriate uses and inform product development. He reports informal idea validation through calls to musicians, athletes and celebrities around the SAG-AFTRA and Writers Guild strikes, rather than a systematic study. The legal role described is advising on paths forward for individual clients and helping shape the platform.
qs: In that first meeting, I walked out and just started dialing musicians and athletes, and celebrities that I have access to, and just start asking them what they thought.
It was right around the time the SAG-AFTRA strikes, and the Writers Guild strike.
We're at the table helping talent with their attorneys, figure out the best path forward for those individuals and allowing them to help us build the right product to meet those needs.

kp.k: Platform revenues combine subscriptions and transaction participation
kp.d: Siegfried describes subscriptions paid by talent and brands for blueprint creation, storage, use and collaboration, plus a percentage of usage or licensing fees when Official AI introduces new commercial relationships. He says most revenue follows demonstrated value to the parties. This is a cross-domain platform pricing model, not a claim about law-firm fees or legal-service delivery.
qs: We're a subscription model. So talent, brands pay for access to our platform.
Not only to create and safely store the blueprint of their likeness or product, but to also leverage it and collaborate with others.

Then when we bring new opportunities to the table, for example, if we bring a shoe company to a modeling agency, through our platform introducing a relationship they didn't have before, we also take a percentage of a usage fee.
We only get paid, the majority of our money is made once we've proven value to all parties.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Dave Siegfried claims that synthetic media can be authentic when consent is verifiable, and that Official AI enables consent-based creation and licensing of people's likenesses.
pts.d: Siegfried describes creating a digital 'blueprint' from as few as 10 images, then using it to generate approved images and video with optional voice models. He says this allows talent and brands to create campaigns despite scheduling constraints, or produce content complementary to existing photography. His authenticity claim concerns authorization of synthetic content, not whether an image records a real event. Official AI is presented as a technology platform, not a provider of legal services.

pts.k: Siegfried claims layered provenance can make authorization, alterations and licensing status inspectable, and predicts platforms will use such checks before distributing content.
pts.d: He describes a current approach combining C2PA manifests with cryptographic signatures, watermarking, fingerprinting and perceptual hashes. He says Official AI can display provenance and basic licensing details, including whether a license has expired. He predicts social platforms will eventually check authenticity at upload, while reactive takedown services will remain necessary. Here verification means content authentication and authorization checking, not human checking of AI-generated legal work.

pts.k: Siegfried argues that generative AI has outgrown existing platform takedown mechanisms and creates a need for both proactive consent tools and reactive removal tools.
pts.d: He characterizes current removal processes as difficult, user-driven and designed for earlier problems or liability mitigation rather than effective responses to AI likeness misuse. Official AI's proposed prevention is expressly directed at people willing to obtain authorization; he does not claim it prevents all malicious misuse.

pts.k: Siegfried presents publicity and image rights as an immediately usable basis for AI consent technology while training-data copyright disputes remain unresolved.
pts.d: He explicitly excludes underlying model-training data from Official AI's focus. He expects that issue to be resolved eventually through markets and courts, without a definite timetable. Meanwhile, he says the company can work within existing likeness-rights laws and adapt as they evolve. He describes attorneys collaborating with talent and the company on a path forward, but makes no prediction about lawyer displacement, staffing or legal fees.

pts.k: Siegfried predicts a hybrid authentication infrastructure with an immutable, openly accessible record, while maintaining that blockchain is unnecessary for the company's current approach.
pts.d: He qualifies the prediction by identifying a trade-off: closed blockchains restrict who can authenticate content, whereas open ones may expose information that should remain private. His proposed infrastructure must allow the public to establish authorization without disclosing confidential license terms.

pts.k: Siegfried claims a consent-based AI platform can facilitate new commercial relationships and compensation for talent, and describes plans to build an 'AI teammate.'
pts.d: He says brands can discover talent, collaborate on synthetic content and pay usage or licensing fees. Official AI charges subscriptions and takes a percentage when it introduces a new commercial opportunity. Its development roadmap is an AI teammate for individuals, brands and advertising consultants; the interview does not specify autonomous capabilities or measurable outcomes for that planned product.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims rest primarily on Siegfried's founder experience, descriptions of product operation and customer interactions, rather than quantified evaluation.
pts.d: Siegfried cites earlier music-licensing and provenance work at Audiosocket, current customer use, and exploratory conversations with musicians, athletes and celebrities during company formation. He invokes C2PA and Adobe content credentials as technical reference points, and uses iTunes as an analogy for a lawful alternative to unauthorized use. No benchmarks, authentication error rates, customer revenue results, measured takedown outcomes or specific legal decisions are supplied. Platform adoption and hybrid blockchain infrastructure are personal forecasts; the interview provides no platform commitments or deployment evidence for them.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The 2025 interview distinguishes claimed present capabilities from loosely timed forecasts, with consent, interoperability and confidentiality as important conditions.
pts.d: Blueprint creation, customer collaboration and licensing-data inspection are described as available at the interview date, about a year and a half after launch. Platform-level authentication is expected 'soon'; copyright resolution and hybrid immutable records are assigned no date. The AI teammate is a development objective funded by a recently closed seed round, not a demonstrated capability. Synthetic authenticity is conditional on verifiable consent, and broad authentication depends on accessible standards that do not reveal private licensing details.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are talent and ordinary individuals, commercial content buyers, their attorneys, platforms and audiences.
pts.d: Siegfried identifies athletes, models, musicians, celebrities and ordinary people as potential users seeking control and compensation for likeness use. Brands, modeling agencies and advertising consultants gain ways to find collaborators and produce authorized content under scheduling constraints. Attorneys are described as advisers helping talent navigate these arrangements and contributing product guidance, not as being replaced. Platforms face authentication and removal demands; audiences are intended to gain access to provenance information. These are media, licensing and identity-protection claims, not claims about the wider structure of legal services.
